lesson.title: When One Outcome Doesn't Touch Another: The Multiplication Rule
lesson.summary: For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) times P(B), because knowing one event happened gives no information at all about the other.
lesson.body:
Two events are independent when knowing that one of them happened gives no new information about whether the other one happened, meaning the probability of the second event stays exactly the same whether or not the first event occurred. When events are independent, the multiplication rule gives a simple way to find the probability that both happen: P(A and B) = P(A) times P(B). This is exactly the missing piece the previous chapter needed, since the general addition rule requires knowing P(A and B) as an input, and independence is the first situation where that joint probability can be computed directly from the two individual probabilities rather than by counting outcomes from a table.

The rule works because independence means B behaves the same way regardless of what happened with A. Picture running the random phenomenon for A first, then separately running the random phenomenon for B. Whatever fraction of the time A happens, call it P(A), that same B still happens its usual fraction of the time, P(B), within that group, because A gave no information that would shift B's odds one way or the other. Multiplying the two probabilities together captures exactly that: the fraction of all trials where A happens, further narrowed down by the unchanged fraction where B also happens. This is fundamentally different from disjoint events from two chapters back, where A happening actually guarantees B did not, the opposite of independence.

Independence shows up naturally whenever one random phenomenon has no physical or logical connection to another. Successive flips of the same coin are independent, since a coin has no memory of its previous landing. Drawing a card, recording it, and then putting it back into a full, reshuffled deck before drawing again keeps the draws independent, since the deck composition resets each time. Independence breaks down, however, the moment one outcome actually changes the conditions for the next one, such as drawing a card and not replacing it, which shrinks the deck and shifts the odds for the second draw, a dependent situation the next chapter addresses directly.

Return to the two coin flip sample space from several chapters back, S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}. The two flips are independent, since the coin has no memory, so the multiplication rule gives P(HH) = P(heads on flip one) times P(heads on flip two) = 1/2 times 1/2 = 1/4. This matches the earlier direct count exactly, since HH was one of four equally likely listed outcomes, each with probability 1/4, confirming that the multiplication rule and the brute force listing approach agree.

The rule extends naturally beyond coins. Suppose, for illustration, a city survey finds that 30 percent of adults exercise regularly and, independently of that, 60 percent of adults own a pet, with no relationship assumed between the two habits. The probability that a randomly selected adult both exercises regularly and owns a pet is P(exercise) times P(pet) = 0.30 times 0.60 = 0.18, or 18 percent. If exercise and pet ownership were not actually independent in real life, meaning owning a pet somehow changed someone's likelihood of exercising, this shortcut would give the wrong answer, which is exactly why checking independence before multiplying matters.

Not every pair of events researchers care about is independent, and pretending they are when they are not produces confidently wrong answers. The next chapter develops the general multiplication rule, which handles dependent events by explicitly accounting for how the first event changes the odds of the second.
